speechtext:
With the picture which my hon. friend from Yale (Mr. Stirling) has drawn of conditions in his district, I quite sympathize. I have some knowledge, not perhaps of that particular district but of conditions at home; I have had personal experience of conditions that arise when ten per cent undertake to defeat the cooperation of ninety per cent. But I am rather afraid that in his endorsation of this bill the hon. gentleman has been animated rather by a desperate desire to get something than by a close examination of the bill itself. I am afraid that the golden apple of this bill will prove to be Dead Sea fruit and turn to ashes in his mouth.
I do not think the hon. member was quite fair to my hon. friend from Last Mountain (Mr. Butcher) or to the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) in suggesting that they argued the matter from the political standpoint. I thought their remarks were singularly dear and that they presented a very graphic picture, and to some extent a
Marketing Act-Mr. Neill

superior picture to that given us by the hon. member for Yale, inasmuch as they confined themselves entirely to the effect of the bill, whereas the hon. member for Yale wandered further afield and spoke in general terms. There are at any rate two items with which I shall deal when I come to them and regarding which may I say with all respect and politeness to him that he read into the measure something that I submit is not there.
Much has been said about the principle of this bill, I suppose there is a principle in it, but it is so obscured and surrounded by unnecessary and, in some cases, almost vicious details, that it is somewhat difficult to find it. To that principle I am in a sense committed, not from any instructions or requests I have received from home,, for I have received none in connection with this bill, but rather that I have on the platform and privately at home endorsed the general idea, talking about the marketing act as it was introduced in Great Britain and saying that possibly the measure which we would adopt in time to come would be along those lines. To that extent I should be very glad to support the principle of this bill if one could disinter the principle from the mass of confusion and details which surround it. But in that case I would have to keep for myself a very large reservation of liberty to vote and work for a very thorough amendment of the bill in committee, and, :f it were not so amended, to vote against it on the third reading more particularly as regards clause 9, which I consider the most vicious one in the whole bill. As, however, the government has a large majority, my vote one way or the other matters not to it; the question is only one between my constituents and myself.
I agree, in fact I more than agree with, I heartily endorse everything said by the hon. member for Last Mountain in his very well thought out presentation of the subject, especially when he stated that if the bill had followed the lines of the British act he would have been prepared to support it. I also agree with the hon. member for Hants-Kings in much of his criticism,, but I differ from him in regard to the principle. I admit the truth of the point he made regarding the experiments tried in various parts of the world in curtailing production by withholding goods from the market in connection with rubber, coffee and so forth, and how they have failed. I suppose we were all brought up to believe the law of supply and demand was one that could never be defeated by any machinery of legislation. But times change and we must move with them, even possibly against a law

that we thought was impregnable. But the conditions on which this bill is based are not exactly similar to those mentioned by the hon. member for Hants-Kings, and even if they were, I say that times change; there is in London a committee sitting, trying to set the price of wheat for the whole world. Does that not give a marked indication of the progress we have made along those lines?
Another argument in favour of the principle of the bill is that if we do not check or regulate our exportation, Great Britain will do it for us and will do it in a way that we do not like. Britain has already intimated to New Zealand that, despite treaties, she must cut down her butter imports. She has advised us politely and by way of negotiations, conversations, rather than by the mailed fist, that we shall have to go slowly on our exportations of cattle and I think we shall very soon find that the same thing will apply as regards our exports of butter to the mother country. The Hon. Mr. Elliot, Minister of Agriculture there, is determined, so far as he can, to make Great Britain self-sufficient from a food standpoint. One cannot blame him, but we shall have to pay some of the price.
Then again, to combat the argument of the hon. member for Hants-Kings, we have some precedents, not only in the British act but also in the New Zealand act, and I am always ready to follow the lead of those two great countries at opposite ends of the world, Britain with her sober, staid, conservative method of making progress slowly, a step at a time, but never going back and always making a success of what she undertakes, and at the other end New Zealand with the finest population on earth, full of optimism, of forward-looking movement, ready to embark on what I might call the very best form of socialistic ideas, and making a success of them. So I say, when I find those two countries uniting on a measure and giving me a precedent, I am willing to follow them a long way. In New Zealand, as far back as 1921 they passed the Meat Export Control Act which gave them absolute control, if necessary, of the whole of the meat. Of course this was only as regards export; it did not deal with domestic consumption except inasmuch as it related to export, but it provided for pooling and a levy on the whole of the produce exported. In 1923 they passed a similar act dealing with dairy produce when again they took power to make a levy on everything exported in order to finance the scheme and they also took power to pool. The scheme must have worked pretty well because that is

Marketing Act-Mr. Neill
ten or twelve years ago and they have not had occasion to change their aot since then. As a matter of fact their act to control meat exports is working very well.
Great Britain put her marketing act into force in 1931 and before much practical organization was done, she passed another one in 1933, which was largely an amplification, an extension and, to some extent, an amendment of the first one. Now pooling was unfortunately omitted from our legislation. The hon. member for Yale read into one of the sections something which he hoped rather than thought would cover that, but I have under my hand the latest advices from British Columbia where the legal authorities say that our measure does not cover pooling and that the local act cannot under our legislation institute pooling either. But pooling is in the British act and also in the New Zealand one.
I think the hon. member for Yale quoted clause 4 as follows:
The board shall, subject to the provisions of this act. have power,
(a) to regulate the time and place of marketing the regulated product.
I have not found any lawyer who is willing to read into that power to pool the marketing of products.
I said that Britain had a marketing act and we might well follow it, but we must remember that Britain differs from us in three very fundamental and important aspects. I want to impress that upon the house. First, Britain is a small, compact country, homogeneous to a large extent in its population, and where every point can be reached easily by wire in a few minutes or by transport in a few hours. That is very important as compared with the great distances in this country. The second is that Britain has one jurisdiction and that is a most important and almost vital matter as compared with our conditions. There is only one body to give orders, to report to and so forth. We have nine and we have also the boards below that. Just imagine the vast possibilities for misunderstandings and disputes that will arise between bodies three or four thousand miles apart in carrying on negotiations and arrangements that in Britain would be dealt with in a matter of minutes.
Another equally important matter is that Britain is an importing country and in that is her safeguard, her bank, her reservoir, her safety valve for any trouble that may happen. She has only to take in the slack and say with a wave of her hand to outside nations: A little less butter or ham or bacon as the case may be. In that way her troubles are solved because she is an importing country. Her policy is destined to stimulate production
and as that production grows, what will she do? She will stop the imports to a proportionate extent; she can do this, so to speak, by a wave of her hand, saying: A little less on the quota, and the whole business goes on smoothly and profitably. What have we? We have power to stop imports, but that would not do us much good. We have power to stop exports, but what good would that do us? I think it always has been found that when you get a government scheme, even if the price is low, it has a security, a certainty and a finality about it so that people will increase their production. The government of Brazil took over their coffee at a very low price and thought there would be no increase in production, but people got in new machinery and increased their production three or four times over because their money was sure. There is no doubt that this scheme will stimulate production, as is the intention in Great Britain and no doubt will be the result here, and what are we to do? We cannot raise our hands and stop importations to meet the case; we have to dispose of that slack in some way that will be very difficult to arrange.
Now I should like to deal with the bill itself for a few moments, not in regard to the details appropriate for discussion in committee but rather in its general aspects. These things, put together, form the reason why one should or should not support the bill itself. This is the most appallingly autocratic bill I ever had in my hand. Outside of Stalin I do not believe any of the dictators in Europe who at least pretend to practise constitutional government would bring forward a measure of this kind. I notice that the definition of natural products includes food or drink wholly or partly manufactured or derived from any such product. I suppose that would include liquor, which is made from grain; I want to use that illustration later on. We turn over the page and come to the dominion marketing board. Under section 3 the governor in council may establish a board to be known as the dominion marketing board, and subsection 2 states:
The board shall consist of such number of persons as the governor in council may from time to time determine-
I wonder if what someone said the other night was true, that this act is only introduced as a gesture and is not meant to be used. I hope that is not so; I do not believe it, but certainly the utter lack of definiteness about many of these matters would lead to that supposition. This board may consist of three or of fifteen people. Is there any civil
Marketing Act-Mr. Neill

service appointment about it; is there any returned soldiers' preference? No; it will be almost as good as the Senate; it will be a home for burned out politicians, and if fifteen is not enough members the government can esaily make it twenty. In connection with our railway board, our tariff board and our pensions board the number of members is mentioned and the salaries are named as well. Here it states that they shall receive such remuneration as the governor in council shall determine. What is the reason for that? In these other important acts which have been passed by this house the salaries of the chairman and of the other members are specified. Here it is provided, apparently, that they shall get such remuneration as they ask. In another subsection it states that the governor in council may authorize certain members of the board to exercise the functions of the board in respect of any product or class of products. I suppose that might mean one member; we might have one man in Canada placed in supreme control of the lumber business, the fish business, the butter business or the liquor business. What possibilities that opens up for campaign funds, does it not? That it is, however; one man may have that power.
There is another point here; I am not a lawyer, and perhaps this may sound ridiculous from a legal standpoint, but I mention it for the consideration of lawyers. The whole of this bill to this point is entirely superfluous; that is, this board is only a buffer, a convenient but expensive buffer between the minister and the real boards called local boards, to which reference is made later on. They are really in the same position as the British boards. There is nothing similar to this dominion board in Great Britain; they have what is here called local boards and the minister deals with those boards. Those boards are the same, as to their origin at least, as the boards that will be created under section 5 of this bill. I maintain that this dominion marketing board is a superfluity.
On the next page I see it is provided that they may regulate the time and place of marketing the regulated product. What product? A board must deal with one or more named products, but this board is not going to do any work of that kind; it is going to be a sort of senate, looking down on the real boards that are doing the work, and we are going to pay for three, five, ten or fifteen men at any price they like to name, while the local boards will do the work. That is not the way it is done in Great Britain.

Then here is the most vicious thing in the act, next to section 9. Under subsection (b) of section 4 the board have the following power:
to exempt from any determination or order any person or class of persons engaged in the production or marketing-
Mark that.
-of the regulated product or any class, variety or grade of such product.
What is the practice under the British system? It is very different. The British system exempts certain people from the scheme, and that is a very different thing. I need not take time to go into the details, but they exempt certain small people from the working of the entire scheme. I find on looking up the act that in the case of dairy produce those having less than four cows are exempt, and that a man selling less than twenty-five eggs at one time is exempt as well. These people are saved all the bother; they do not have to register or go through any of the formalities; the government do not have to clutter up their records with them, and it is so much fairer to everyone. But what is to be the system here? This board is to be given power to exempt from any determination or order an individual or individuals engaged in producing or marketing. It might be that only one man will be exempt; the board might say, "We are going to prohibit the exportation of butter for two or three weeks" but by accident Tom Jones may be exempt from that determination. What would that be worth to him? It might be worth a small fortune. Under the British system that could not happen. In order to keep them satisfied with their lot the section hands on the railways throughout the country are encouraged to keep a cow, a pig, a few chickens and so on. They will have to sit up nights in order to make these returns; they will have to be registered and so on, with all the trouble involved. The greatest danger, of course, is that somebody with a pull may just happen to be exempt from the marketing order that may be made, and if he is an exporter himself he will make a very good thing out of it.
Further on in the act there is provision for lending money for the construction or operation of facilities for preserving, storing or conditioning the product. Every man who has a root house for potatoes or anything else will want the government to pay for it; every man who has not a roothouse will want the government to build one. All the creameries will want some help from the government. There is also provision for research

Marketing Act-Mr. Neill
work. That may be all right in Great Britain, but it has nothing to do with this bill. We deal with research work in another way in this country.	_
Then we come to subsection (f), which states:
to require any or all persons engaged in the production or marketing of the regulated product to register their names, addresses^ and occupations with the board, or to obtain a licence from the board-
All these men with one cow and a pig have to get licences from the board, and those licences are subject to cancellation on the say so of the board for the violation of any provision. Is that the system in Great Britain? It is not. There they outline the penalties in their scheme; violations are punished by fines, and they do not go so far as cancelling the licence of the individual. And as the hon. member for Last Mountain pointed out last night, they make provision for looking after the consumer. There is a consumers' committee, who see that the scheme does not injure the consumer. Above that there is another committee which has power to take action and change the scheme if it finds any abuse or injury being committed. Is there anything of that kind in our act? If there is I have not found it. Again it is provided that people must send in all these returns. Fancy the poor section hand sitting up at night asking his wife how much she churned in March and how much in April, because if he does not know that the whole return is upset.
Then subsection 2 reads:
The board may collect charges for services rendered,
(a)	in respect of all or any portion of the
regulated product marketed under its direction, and	. .
(b)	if it cooperates or acts conjointly with any marketing board or agency established under the law of any province, in respect of all or any portion of the product subject to regulation by such provincial board or agency.
I do not find much fault with that except that it leads to confusion and a great deal of bookkeeping. Then, right near the end of section 4, half way through the whole bill, we come to the first mention of the real scheme. The word "scheme" is noticed for the first time in the reference to the board. At section 5 I find the following:
A representative number of persons engaged in the production and marketing or the production or marketing of a natural product may petition the governor in council to approve a scheme for the regulation of the marketing of such natural product by a local board under the supervision of the board.
This is the real thing; this is the real act. This is the thing which corresponds to the British board, namely that which we call the local board. The procedure is to petition, and one minister, remember, considers whether that petition is good, or whether those men are representative. My friend and I may call ourselves representative, and yet we may not be. The British system requires that they shall be substantially representative. The minister makes the decision, just one man,- just the minister. If he is satisfied and considers the petition satisfactory he does not have to give any explanation. When the minister goes to the House of Commons in Great Britain he has to give reasons why he thinks his decision is all right, and he has to put his views in writing. But in this country, according to this bill, he does not need to do anything at all, except-consider. If he considers the thing is O.K. and the persons engaged are sufficiently representative the scheme shall be referred to the board. In that connection I shall but refer to the foreword to the British act. This is what it says:
Every scheme shall be administered by a board elected by the producers.
Are our schemes going to be administered by boards elected by the producers? Not at all. We can elect a lot of Chinese laundry-men, if we wish, and it would be quite all right.
Then I shall turn to some of the provisions pointed out last night by the hon. member for Last Mountain. I shall touch upon them only briefly. This is what -the British minister has to do: He has to get the petition, and then he has to publish it for a period of six weeks. Then he holds a public meeting to see if anybody wishes to kick about it. Then he lays it before each house of parliament, and along with it must be a copy of the evidence which convinced him that the scheme was suitable. His action must be the same both before the House of Commons and before the House of Lords. Then they have to provide for a board to administer the scheme. The men- who run it have to be elected in such manner as -may be provided by the scheme, and they must be registered producers. After all that is done, namely after the House of Commons and the House of Lords have O.K.'d the procedure, the minister approves the scheme, but he suspends it for about two months, within which time he takes a plebiscite or a poll of all the registered producers. If sixty-six per cent do not vote for it the whole thing is off, and if less than fifty per cent vote it is closed off automatic-
Marketing Act-Mr. Neill

ally. These are some of the safeguards imposed by the British government, but which are wholly lacking in the measure before this House of Commons. Under this measure the scheme needs only the O.K. of the minister who thinks that Tom Jones and his friends are decent fellows-and he lets it go at that.
In order to give a further illustration I should like to make a quotation. Apparently in the British parliament they have introductions to their bills, and in this instance I quote from introductory remarks:
The procedure regulating initiation and control of schemes is democratic in character.
Can we say that about our measure? It continues:
By whomsoever they may be prepared, schemes may be submitted only by producers of the product concerned; moreover, there must be a poll, on which all affected producers can vote, before any scheme comes into full operation. Similarly, democratic control in the administration of every scheme is assured by the fact that the board, i.e., the administrative body entrusted with the administration of the scheme, is composed of the elected representatives of registered producers.
How very far distant is that from anything to be found in the measure before us. Democracy?-democracy appears to have been forgotten when this bill was drafted.
Then we come to some of the provisions to be found in the measure. I find that every scheme shall state "the number of persons who shall comprise the local board and the basis of their selection." It may be the president of the Liberal or the Conservative association, so far as this regulation is concerned. They do not need to be representatives of producers. The stipulation is merely as to the "basis of their selection." Selection?-they may agree upon an appointment by the minister. It does not say "election" but "basis of their selection." That is where the hon. member for Yale went wrong. He stated that they would be elected by the producers. Probably the hon. member hopes so, but certainly there is no guarantee of it in the measure.
Then section 6 indicates that the framers of the bill have awakened at last, and have thought of giving some publicity to the thing. In that connection section 6 states:
When a scheme has been approved by the governor in council, the minister shall give public notice thereof in the Canada Gazette.
That is, when the scheme has gone through the successive stages of the minister, the board and the council, this action will be taken Why not do it before the scheme is
[Mr. Neill.)
approved? Would that not be a good idea, when they are going to publish it afterwards in the Gazette? So much for Canadian democracy.
Then in section 8 we find a provision which at the present time I shall not go into. It is a provision for extending the power of any local board, but there is no check on them, and no suggestion of how it is to be done. It is just simply on the say so of the minister, or if the governor in council is satisfied with the recommendation of the minister. That is all that is required. I may remind the house that in Great Britain one has to go through pages of forms, if a scheme is to be substituted, amended or extended. The same performance has to be followed which is followed in an original case. One has to go through the House of Lords, through the House of Commons and so on. Here the extension may be made, heaven knows to what extent, simply if the minister himself is satisfied.
Now we come to section 9-and that is the section which I consider the most vicious in its import. I cannot see how the minister, a man whom I respect, with whom I have no trouble at all and with whom I never had a harsh word, could sanction this section. Much as I respect him I cannot understand why he has allowed section 9 to creep into the bill. I do suggest that the progress of the measure would be greatly helped if section 9 were eliminated. It is as follows:
Notwithstanding that no petition in relation to any natural product has been filed, the minister may if he-
-think it is necessary, put in a scheme of his own. If he thinks it is necessary he can draw7 it up himself. Because he believes some trade to be injuriously affected he may propose a scheme for the marketing of the products of that trade. He does not need even to take it before the board. He takes it to the governor in council, who, in turn, approves of the scheme and authorizes the board to administer such scheme directly or through any agency which it may establish. It is not limited even to the formalities of the rest of the bill, but is given entirely to any agency which may be established.
Let me suggest this: Everything is going along smoothly and quietly in a certain industry, but all of a sudden out of a blue sky the minister takes the notion-or some minister; I shall not refer to any particular minister, because he is not named-some person makes a suggestion to the minister who says, suddenly, " We will have a scheme about

Marketing Act-Mr. Neill
that; I shall draw it up and I shall have the government approve of it"-which, of course, is a mere formality-"and then I will appoint a board, and the board will appoint Tom Jones to run it." The whole of that industry may be run by that man, without warning or notice, except that publication will be made in the Gazette after everything is all cut and dried. The expression in the bill is: "through any agency which it may establish."
Then, section 12, subsection 2, is as follows:
The governor in council may, by order or regulation published in the Canada Gazette,
(a) provide that any natural product shall not be expoi-ted from Canada without a licence.
That, of course, is a necessary provision, and I agree with it. But I notice that the British act of 1933, which I have before me, gives the same provision, namely, that the government may prohibit the importation of any particular article. In the British act, however, there are four pages of safeguards. If any hon. member questions my statement may I say that I have the measure before me, and he may see for himself that there are four pages, as I have indicated. But here it is simply done by the governor in council.
I visualize the situation like this: The governor in council may provide that a certain natural product shall not be exported from Canada. In the constituency which I represent there are many trollers, that is, fishermen who troll for salmon. At this time of the year their market is entirely in the United States, in Seattle. I need not go into why that is so, but I simply state that that is the case. They could get a market in the canneries, but it would be an inferior market. The canneries do not particularly need it because it is not good for canning, but they could handle it as fresh fish. Suppose a couple of canners got together and, after using influence, got the board to decide that none of that fish was to be exported. What would be the situation of those trollers? What remedy would they have? Under the British act when a man is aggrieved by its operation he can go before two arbitrators appointed under the act. You will find all that in the 1931 act, I think it is. He can go before two arbitrators and get a ready form of arbitration. There is nothing of that kind here. No; he simply has to take his medicine.
The minister said that he thought there were three requisites for this act, and that was that it should be sound, simple and practical. What a travesty on the English language if you call this bill sound, simple and practical! It is a travesty on truth and justice and common sense to call this bill sound, simple
'and practical. If I had two bitter enemies I would not wish them a worse fate than to put one to run this act and the other to try to make a living under it. It would be a case indeed of "Judah is avenged of her children."
My time is nearly up, but I would like to say a word on part II. That is the less important part of the bill. It is the part that deals with investigations into spreads. The first part deals with people charging a commission; the second is concerned with the people handling; and the third provides that the minister may at the request of the board or on his own initiative institute an investigation of the spread on any natural product. Why natural products? Why not any product at all? A lot of evidence has been given before the price spreads committee dealing with the horrible spread and the slum conditions and sweated wages of workers on manufactured articles. As this bill is dealing with spreads, why not deal with spreads in manufactured articles also? I suggest that if it is going to inquire into the spread on natural products, the bill might as well also be applied to the spreads in manufactured articles so as to give the consumer a little look in.
Section 18 of the bill says, a regulated product. Surely it should be natural product, any natural product, in fact, any product at all. Then section 21 provides that every person who receives a spread that is excessive shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding $5,000 or two years imprisonment in the case of an individual, and to a penalty of not exceeding $10,000 in the case of a corporation. That is put in just as window dressing. They might as well have said ten million dollars. Is there any chance of any company paying a fine of $10,000 for an offence under this act? Would it be fair that any individual should have to pay a fine of $5,000 for some very petty offence against this act?
Another thing. A spread is a rather difficult thing to determine. What is a fair spread to me might be a much more expensive spread to my neighbour. By improved methods, greater energy and good management one man may be able to handle an article at a lower cost. If his case is selected as the criterion the other man is going to pay a fine of $5,000 simply because he uses obsolete machinery or does not have the same energy or good management as the other fellow. I do not say that the man with the antiquated methods should be taken as the standard, but I do say that he should not be fined $5,000 judged by the standard of the man with more modern methods and better management.
Marketing Act-Mr. Brown

I suppose, Mr. Speaker, that some will say that I have been simply tearing this thing to pieces and trying to attack it in a political way. I have nothing to gain in a political way by attacking this bill. It is not an issue in my district, and I can take as impersonal and unprejudiced a view of it as I ever did of anything. But as I see it, this bill needs not an architect but a wrecker. Let us tear it down and build it up again. All praise and credit to the minister for the conception behind the act, but let us have an act that really regulates and that will be effective in the interests of the men described by my hon. friend from Yale and my hon. friend from Hants-Kings. Then no one will be more willing to support it and promote its passage through the house than myself.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think there will be general agreement with the statement of the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) that this is one of the most important bills that has been introduced into the house in many years. It is generally recognized now that agriculture is the industry upon which the prosperity of Canada must be based, and the marketing of agricultural products is a matter that has given great concern to the farmers during very many years.
In the early days of our fanner organizations in the west, when we undertook to concern ourselves with the marketing of our produce we were practically told by those interested in the trade that the marketing was none of our business, that our business was to produce, and they would take care of the marketing. Well, we did not see it that way. We thought it was a matter of very great concern to us not only to make two blades of grass grow where one grew before but to see that what we produced was put on the market at the highest profit to ourselves. So we proceeded to consider ways and means of marketing, and we did establish cooperative institutions that have functioned with greater or less success, some of them with a great deal of success, and some of them unfortunately proving apparently a failure.
I wish at the outset to pay a tribute to the two hon. members who started the discussion of this bill, the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Butcher) and the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley). With their keen legal minds they have analyzed the provisions of this bill and thoroughly exposed its weaknesses, so that it is only necessary for those of us who follow to deal with some of the details and point out some of the situations that are likely to arise and that undoubtedly will arise if the provisions of this bill are put into effect.

I wish I could pay a similar tribute to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir). So far as explaining the principle of the bill is concerned his speech was very disappointing. Not only did he not deal with the details of the bill, but he did not even remotely touch upon its principles. I can come to only one conclusion, though it may be a wrong one, and that is that this bill was something that was handed to him and that he was told to put it across. But in some respects the minister's speech was an excellent one, and under certain circumstances I could have listened to it with a great deal of interest. The minister showed a very clear understanding of the difficulties that have confronted the farmers in handling their produce profitably. Being a farmer he clearly recognizes the handicaps that have been imposed upon us, but in my judgment he completely failed to set forth even in a general way the principles which he proposes to apply through this bill to remedy the present difficulties.
The minister told us that he had received many communications from all over Canada endorsing this bill. I am not at all surprised at that. The attitude of the farmers, unfortunately, and the same may be said of other sections of the population as well, has been such that during the hard times through which we are passing they are ready to accept almost anything that holds out the slightest hope of better conditions. They are ready to try almost anything, and so I am not at all surprised that a general expression of approval of this bill should have come from many sources. But it must be remembered that these expressions of approval have been founded on a very insufficient knowledge of the bill, and I think we may fairly ask what, after all, are men's opinions worth who only know that it was the intention of the government to bring in a bill to facilitate the marketing of farm produce and who know actually nothing about the details of the measure proposed. It may be that there are institutions here and there which have received copies of the bill and, therefore, are in position to express a measure of intelligent opinion upon it, but I am quite satisfied that many of these expressions of approval have come from men who are not sufficiently informed of the contents of the bill and of how far-reaching it is in some respects. Undoubtedly the avowed purpose of the bill is one of which we must approve; according to the title it is an act to improve the methods and practices of marketing of natural products in Canada and in export trade, and to

Marketing Act-Mr. Brown
make further provisions in connection therewith.
I have not the slightest doubt-I am speaking now of men in the prairie provinces where our wheat is grown

that many men are of the opinion that this bill is to provide something like the old wheat board which was established to handle the crop of 1919. I think we can pay a tribute to that board and say that it was a magnificent success under the guidance of Mr. James Stewart. I believe that gentleman served on the board without recompense, and he was supported by men who were well acquainted with the grain trade. Undoubtedly that board handled that crop to the satisfaction of the farmers. If I remember rightly, we received an initial payment of $222$ or $2.25 and a final payment of 48 cents per bushel. We were quite satisfied. There was a demand that that board be continued. There was a mistaken feeling that such a board could continue to do for us what Mr. James Stewart had done with the crop of 1919. I have no doubt that remembering the satisfactory manner in which that board functioned, many are looking forward to the establishing of a board which will bring about the conditions which prevailed at that time. However, I think we can put out of our minds the thought that any wheat board could do for us to-day what that wheat board did under the circumstances which prevailed at that time. It is not at all surprising that expressions of approval should come from many different sources.
The minister referred to some of our cooperative efforts and he gave some of the reasons why he thought some of those experiments had failed. I agree with most of the reasons he gave, and I certainly agree with him when he says that one of the main causes of failure was the putting into positions of business management those who had made a success as propagandists. I do not intend to mention specific cases but we have good reason to know that some of the mistakes made in a business way were made by men who had no business capacity but who were capable propagandists. It is a good thing to have propagandists for a cause but the fact that a man is able to get up on a platform and expatiate upon the benefits of a particular line of conduct does not mean that he is capable of handling such a business as the selling of wheat. I have had men tell me that they did not consider there was anything to the selling of wheat and that in their opinion such an operation did not require a clever man. There are those who use the statement of the former Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) to the effect that wheat sold itself. At
the time that the former Minister of Trade and Commerce said that, that statement was largely true. It did not require any great activity on the part of the government to sell wheat, but things have changed.

It is just as true as
if you had said it.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I think the minister would have said the same thing at that time.
There was another reason given by the minister for the failure of the cooperatives and it is one to which too much weight must not be attached. He said that many of these cooperatives failed because they did not have one hundred per cent control. The hon. member for Yale has stated the case of the fruit growers very clearly and in most moderate language. We always listen to what he says with a great deal of interest, and I have no doubt that what he said with regard to the difficulties which confronted those growers in the marketing of their fruit is absolutely true. I have no doubt that the situation which prevailed in Vancouver with regard to milk is as has been described, but we must not carry such arguments too far. There are those who say that the failure of the wheat pool was attributable to the fact that they did not have one hundred per cent control. I do not intend to go into the causes at any great length, but I state most emphatically that whatever they were, they were not attributable in any sense to the fact that they did not have one hundred per cent control. At the time that the pool was on the verge of bankruptcy, if not already bankrupt, it was a strange attitude for the executives to take when they said that if they had only had one hundred per cent control they could have handled the thing much better. I do not want to be unjust in my criticism of the pool but in my judgment there is no doubt that had the fluctuations in the grain trade been normal the pool would have continued to function with satisfaction. But it could not stand up against the tremendous drop which occurred in the price of wheat, especially when the initial payment had been more than that ultimately received for the wheat. All I ask of any body of officials is that they be honest and face the facts and not make undue claims for powers which it would have been impossible for them to exercise under any condition.

Marketing Act-Mr. Brown
There is another cause for the failure of our cooperatives, and it is one of the weaknesses of democracy. One of the weaknesses of our cooperative institutions is the unwillingness to pay for good service. I think I have heard the former Minister of Agriculture complain that he lost some of his best officials because he was not allowed to pay a remuneration high enough to retain them, and unfortunately it is still true of our cooperative institutions that there is an unwillingness to pay for the service of good men. I remember very well that when we organized the first large grain handling company in the west, the Grain Growers Grain company, one man said that he would manage it for a thousand dollars a year. It might have been managed for one year and there would never have been a second. That is undoubtedly one of the reasons for the failure of our cooperative companies.
There is another reason which is perhaps pertinent to this discussion-the disposition to want to pull down existing institutions and to establish something new. We have that disposition manifest not only in our farmers' cooperatives but in governmental institutions.

speechtext: We want to change the government.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
That is always in order, I suppose. But we have suggestions to-day that instead of working with the economic system we have, for example, we must entirely dispense with it, overthrow it and establish an entirely new system. And so we had this in our marketing institutions; the old system must go; it could not possibly exist side by side with the new, and anyone who suggested that we must go slow and experiment with the new before completely discarding the old was sneered at and scoffed at as a man opposed to all the farmers' interests. And that practically constitutes one of the reasons why our cooperative institutions have not had the measure of success that we should like.
If it is agreeable, Mr. Speaker, I would move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
